tldr: Van de Ven argues that every abstraction layer is a trade-off, and gives a model of cohesion, coupling (depth times connectivity), distance and volatility for deciding when hexagonal architecture is worth its cost.
summary: Ties van de Ven, a software quality expert at Alliander who reviews code for about 200 teams, presents a mental model developed with a colleague. His metaphor is a bag of Fruittella: every wrapper has a purpose, but all of them are in the way when you want the candy, that is, when you need to understand how a request is actually handled. Layers are added for two reasons: to avoid depending on something, or so that other components' changes don't break you. Both have limits. You can't escape a dependency, only move it (JDBC, Hibernate, Spring Data, a homegrown framework). Abstractions leak (@NativeQuery). Mappers protect against representational changes like a renamed column, but not against information loss like a dropped one. In his war story, a year of abstractions turned out to move messages between two Kafka topics, and he replaced it in an afternoon.

He then defines the three concepts. Distance runs from a blank line in a function up to a different company. It lowers local cognitive load and helps teams and deployment, but raises global cognitive load and the cost of change. Cohesion has levels: accidental (utils folders), logical (controllers/services/repositories folders), model, and the target, functional cohesion, meaning one component per use case such as "place order". To get there, think in state changes: input, then validated, enriched and solved input, each with its own domain type, so the type system enforces the order of steps.

Coupling has a depth: intrusive (reflection, casting an interface to an implementation), functional (shared mutable state, files dropped for another process, classes that always change together in git history), and contract coupling. A Java interface with one implementation is not a stronger contract, just more distance. Contracts are also incomplete: performance and security expectations, or an unmodifiable List.add throwing, are rarely written down. Connectivity is fan-in and fan-out. Keep your own contract weak and demand strong contracts from what you depend on. His formula: coupling is depth times connectivity, spaghettification adds the cohesion gap, and pain is spaghettification times volatility. Hexagonal architecture scores well on cohesion and contract coupling but adds a lot of distance, which costs money when nothing changes or when a breaking change runs through every layer.
keyPoints: Abstraction layers relocate dependencies rather than remove them, and often take away features the underlying implementation offers.
Mapping layers protect only against representational changes (renamed fields), not information loss (dropped columns or tables).
Cohesion levels, worst to best: accidental, logical (layered folders), model, functional (one component per use case).
Model a process as named state transitions with their own domain types so the compiler enforces valid ordering, which gives functionally cohesive components.

Coupling depth runs from intrusive through functional (often caused by shared mutable state or temporal coupling) to contract coupling. A single-implementation Java interface adds distance, not contract strength.
Contracts are always incomplete: non-functional expectations such as latency are implicit and can break consumers.
Coupling = depth x connectivity, so high depth is tolerable with low fan-in. Architecture pain = spaghettification x volatility, so a messy codebase that never changes isn't a priority.
Hexagonal architecture scores well on functional cohesion and contract coupling but adds distance, so it costs more when there is no change or when a change loses information.
takeaways: Before adding an interface or layer, name the concrete change it protects against and check whether that change is likely.
Remove interfaces that have only one implementation and no module-boundary purpose. Mock concrete classes instead.
Look at git history for classes that always change together to find hidden functional coupling.
Spend refactoring effort where volatility is high, not on stable legacy code that nobody changes.
Restructure god classes into use-case components by mapping the state changes they perform.

quotes.text: You can never escape a dependency. You can just relocate it.
If you ever see an architecture diagram, the blocks are cohesion and the arrows are coupling.
Architecture is only there to make changes easier, and if you don't have changes, then you don't need architecture.

watchIf: You have inherited or are designing a layered or hexagonal Java codebase and want a vocabulary for arguing which abstractions actually earn their keep.
